study_identification_part.si4_title: Lifespan Normative Models of White Matter Fractional Anisotropy: Applications to Early Psychosis

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The study clearly states its objectives in the abstract and introduction. The research hypotheses/questions are explicitly provided: (i) develop normative models of FA across major white matter tracts using large dataset; (ii) investigate white matter FA in early psychosis to map both group level differences and individual deviations; (iii) illustrate the value of normative models for multi-modal data fusion; (iv) release all models to the community. The purpose of applying normative modeling is clearly described as providing a precision framework to quantify deviations from expected norms at the individual level, capture deviation profiles in a single patient, and bridge the translational gap by providing tailored tools that capture disease risk and progression. Both criteria are fully satisfied.
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text: The aims of this study are to: (i) develop normative models of Fractional Anisotropy (FA), the most widely used diffusion metric in neuroimaging [17], across major white matter tracts using a large dataset of over 25,000 healthy individuals across a broad age range... (ii) investigate white matter FA in early psychosis... (iii) we aim to illustrate the value of normative models for multi-modal data fusion... (iv) we release all models freely to the community... Normative modelling provides a precision framework that has emerged as a promising tool in this endeavour [6], [7], [8]. By comparing brain imaging data against large reference cohorts, this method allows us to quantify deviations from expected norms at the individual level.

nm5_data_preprocessing.supporting_text: The processing of these datasets followed harmonized FSL-based pipelines, summarized in Figure 1A. Initially, pre-processing was performed: B0 intensity normalization, correction for EPI distortions, eddy-current-induced and movement corrections. These corrections were executed using the HCP-pipeline [42] for the HCP datasets while the UKB dataset was already processed according to the UKB documentation [43]. Subsequently, we estimated the DTI model using DTIfit on the lowest shell value in order to extract the fractional anisotropy (FA) values. Following this, we ran Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) [44] on the FA images... Finally, segmentation was conducted using the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) atlas [45]... In line with our prior work [46] we refit the models after excluding gross outliers having deviations larger than 5 standard deviations from the mean (Figure 1C)... the gold standard for diffusion data quality control remains visual inspection

(2) Quantitative thresholds are reported - the study sets z-score thresholds at ±2.6 (corresponding to p=0.01) to identify extreme deviations. (3) Clinical implications of deviation patterns are discussed - the study discusses relationships with symptoms (msCCA analysis identifying associations with PANSS scores, particularly cognitive factor), identifies specific regions (right uncinate fasciculus, bilateral thalamus), and acknowledges limitations. However, the interpretation is somewhat incomplete - while the study identifies that positive weights in uncinate fasciculus might suggest compensatory role, it acknowledges uncertainty ('although we cannot rule out that this finding may also reflect other factors such as crossing fibres'). The discussion addresses heterogeneity but could be more explicit about the biological meaning of FA deviations.
